title: The ESPRIT Algorithm Under High Noise: Optimal Error Scaling and Noisy Super-Resolution
authors: Zhiyan Ding (UC Berkeley), Ethan Epperly (Caltech), Lin Lin (UC Berkeley and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory), Ruizhe Zhang (Simons Institute)
abstract: Subspace-based signal processing techniques, such as the Estimation of Signal Parameters via Rotational Invariant Techniques (ESPRIT) algorithm, are popular methods for spectral estimation. These algorithms can achieve the so-called super-resolution scaling under low noise conditions, surpassing the well-known Nyquist limit. However, the performance of these algorithms under high-noise conditions is not as well understood. Existing state-of-the-art analysis indicates that ESPRIT and related algorithms can be resilient even for signals where each observation is corrupted by statistically independent, mean-zero noise of size $\order(1)$, but these analyses only show that the error $\epsilon$ decays at a slow rate $\epsilon=\mathcal{\tilde{O}}(n^{-1/2})$ with respect to the cutoff frequency $n$ (i.e., the maximum frequency of the measurements). In this work, we prove that under certain assumptions, the ESPRIT algorithm can attain a significantly improved error scaling $\epsilon = \mathcal{\tilde{O}}(n^{-3/2})$, exhibiting noisy super-resolution scaling beyond the Nyquist limit $\epsilon = \mathcal{O}(n^{-1})$ given by the Nyquist--Shannon sampling theorem. We further establish a theoretical lower bound and show that this scaling is optimal. Our analysis introduces novel matrix perturbation results, which could be of independent interest.

C. Related work
There is a long list of algorithms and theoretical results
have been developed for spectral estimation problems
under various assumptions: Approaches include Prony’s
method [30], [31]; subspace-based methods such as ESPRIT [29], [24], [25], [17], MUSIC [3], [32], [25],
and the matrix pencil method [33], [20]; optimizationbased methods [22], [23], [34], [19], [35]; sparse Fourier
transform methods [36], [26], [37]; Fourier interpolation [38], [39], [40]; and tensor decomposition-based
methods [41], [42], to name a few. Among these works,
a substantial body of research [25], [24], [43], [44],
[45], [20], [23], [34], [35], [26], [37], [41] is dedicated
to the classical “super-resolution” regime. This regime
prioritizes identifying the smallest n required to achieve
high precision, operating under the assumption of small
noise. In particular, when µtail = 0 and Ej = O (poly(ϵ)),
setting n = Θ(1/∆z ) is enough for achieving ϵ-accuracy.
Although the super-resolution regime only requires a
small n that is independent of the precision ϵ, the constraints of this regime may be unrealistic in certain realworld applications. For example, in quantum computing,
energy estimation problems [17], [19], [12], [15], [16],
where the goal is to estimate fj accurately, often involve
signals affected by non-dominant signals and random
noise of order O (1) with zero expectation. In this case, the
classical super-resolution type assumption n = Θ(1/∆z )
is no longer adequate. To tackle this challenge, significant
research has been done using approaches based on sparse
